answers.workingTitle: Charge for the Bridge, Not the Bus
answers.format: op-ed for the city's daily paper
answers.audience: Port Ellery commuters and the twelve council members who vote next month
answers.goal: persuade undecided council members to pass the six-dollar downtown congestion charge unamended
answers.constraints: under 800 words; no personal attacks on named councillors
answers.successSignal: a councillor could repeat the core argument and the ring-fencing condition in two sentences

draftText:
Every weekday morning, roughly forty thousand cars cross the Harbour Bridge into downtown Port Ellery, and almost every one of them carries a single person. The city has spent two decades trying to fix this with carrots. It has widened the bridge approach twice, added a bus lane that is routinely full of cars, and built a park-and-ride that sits half empty because the bus from it takes longer than driving. None of this has worked, and the reason is simple: driving downtown is free at the moment of decision, and anything free at the moment of decision will be overused.

The council will vote next month on a downtown congestion charge of six dollars per weekday entry. It should pass it, and it should resist the temptation to water it down.

The case rests on a plain fact about behaviour. When something costs nothing at the point of use, people treat it as if it costs nothing at all, even when the road, the air and their own mornings are paying for it. A charge does not punish drivers. It asks them to see the price that was always there. That is the whole argument.

Cities that have tried this have not regretted it. When Stockholm introduced its charge, traffic into the centre fell by about a fifth and stayed down. London's charge cut congestion in its first year and funded a bus network that still carries the people the charge priced off the road. Closer to home, Verenport's cordon charge cut peak-hour crossings by 31 percent in eighteen months and raised 44 million dollars for transit, and Verenport is a city of almost exactly our size, with a harbour, a single bridge, and a downtown that used to be a car park at nine in the morning.

The main objection is that a charge is regressive: six dollars means more to a hospital cleaner than to a lawyer. This is true, and it is also beside the point, because the cleaner is far more likely to be on the bus already, and the bus is the thing the charge pays for.

A second objection says the charge will kill downtown retail. The evidence for this is thin. Shoppers do not come downtown because parking is pleasant; they come because the shops are there, and they will keep coming on a bus that runs on time. The retailers who have raised the alarm are, in my experience, mostly the ones with the largest car parks.

It is also worth remembering, and this cannot be stressed enough, that the problem we are dealing with here is one that affects everybody in this city, whether or not they personally own a car or drive one, and that the costs of doing nothing are costs that we are all already paying in one form or another, every single day, whether we notice them or not.

What the charge needs in order to work is honesty about where the money goes. Every dollar should be ring-fenced for the bus and ferry network, published quarterly, and audited. The council's draft does this. Members should not let it be amended into a general revenue measure, because the moment the charge looks like a tax, it will be fought like one.

Here is what success looks like. A bridge that moves at eight in the morning. A bus lane with buses in it. A park-and-ride whose shuttle is faster than the car it replaces. A downtown where a delivery van can find the kerb. None of these things is exotic. All of them exist in cities that decided the road was worth something.

The council should pass the charge, pass it whole, and give it three years before anyone is allowed to call it a failure. Driving downtown will cost six dollars. Not driving downtown will finally be worth something. That trade is the whole argument, and it is a good one.

problem: A seventy-word paragraph of throat-clearing that says congestion costs everyone; it should be one plain sentence or go.

answers.audience: readers of literary short fiction
answers.goal: put the reader inside Nell's head at the moment she chooses silence, and make the choice feel earned
answers.constraints: under 900 words; stay in Nell's point of view
answers.successSignal: a reader believes a nine-year-old would make this choice and is frightened for her

draftText:
Nell had been told to count the seconds between the flashes, and she counted them the way she had been taught, with a "Mississippi" after each number, though she had never seen the Mississippi and privately doubted it existed. Four. The light swung round and went out over the water and came back. Four again. Her father said that was how a sailor knew which light he was looking at, because every lighthouse in the world had its own time, like a heartbeat, and a sailor who knew the heartbeats could tell where he was in the dark from forty miles out.

She was nine. It was the first night he had let her sit up in the lamp room, and she had promised not to touch anything, and she had kept the promise for almost an hour.

The lamp itself was behind her, inside its glass, turning on its bath of mercury with a sound like a very slow clock. Her father was below, winding the weight. She could hear the chain going up through the tower in jerks, and his breath between the jerks, and under that the sea, which was the sound she had stopped hearing years ago and had to remember to listen for, the way you have to remember to notice that you are breathing.

Out on the water there was a ship. She saw its lights first, red and green, and then the dark shape between them, and she counted it as she counted everything: a ship, one Mississippi, still there. It was closer than ships usually came. Her father had said the rocks ran out a mile from the point and that was why the light was here, to tell the ships about the rocks, and this ship did not seem to have been told.

She should have called down. She knew that. She thought of the chain going up and her father's breath, and she thought that if she called down he would come up and look and say it was nothing, a fishing boat, and then he would not let her sit up again, and so she watched the ship instead, and counted, and the light went round.

Thomas, winding the weight, had been thinking about the girl's mother, which he did most nights at about this hour, when the work was mechanical and the mind went where it wanted. He did not hear the ship. He did not hear anything but the chain. He was thinking that the girl had her mother's way of looking at a thing as if it owed her an explanation, and that it would get her into trouble, and that he would not be there for all of it.

The ship's green light went out. Nell waited for it to come back and it did not, and she understood, in the slow way that a child understands things that are too large, that the ship had turned, and that the side of it she could see now was the side with no light on it, and that it was turning toward the rocks.

She went to the top of the stairs. She did not call. She stood at the top of the stairs with her hand on the rail, which was cold, and which she was not supposed to touch, and she looked down into the dark of the tower and listened to the chain, and she thought very clearly, and in words, for the first time in her life: if I say nothing, this is mine.

The sea was very calm that night, calmer than it had been for a month, and the sky was clear and there was no wind at all, and the stars were out over the water in their thousands, and the whole of the bay lay under them as still as a plate, and the ship went on turning.

Below her, the chain stopped. Her father's breath stopped with it, and then there was his voice, coming up the tower, saying her name, not loudly, the way he said it when he already knew something was wrong. She did not answer. The light went round. Four Mississippi. The ship had no lights at all now, and she could not see it, and she could not stop seeing it.

answers.audience: early-stage founders and operators choosing what to build
answers.goal: argue that vertical software beats horizontal software and give founders a decision rule
answers.constraints: under 900 words; claims about companies must be checkable
answers.successSignal: a founder can state the thesis and the decision rule in one breath

draftText:
The best software companies of the next decade will not be built for everyone. They will be built for dentists, or freight brokers, or the people who run car washes, and they will be worth more than the horizontal tools they replace. This is not a prediction about niches. It is a prediction about where the margin went.

For twenty years the standard advice was to build the general tool. Make the spreadsheet, the CRM, the project tracker, and let every industry adapt it. The logic was that a big market beats a small one, and that a tool used by every company would be worth more than a tool used by one kind. The logic was right as long as the hard part was building the software. It is no longer the hard part.

What is hard now is knowing the customer. A freight broker does not want a CRM. She wants to know which of her forty carriers will actually show up on Thursday, and she wants the software to already know that a load from Harrowfield to the port needs a tarp and a driver with a hazmat endorsement. The general tool can be configured to do this, by someone, eventually. The vertical tool does it on the first day, because the people who built it used to be freight brokers.

Look at the companies that have actually compounded. Toast started as a restaurant point-of-sale and became the restaurant's bank. ServiceTitan sells to plumbers and is worth more than most of the horizontal tools its customers used to patch together. Procore owns construction. In each case the company began by solving one workflow completely and then found that the customer, having trusted it with the workflow, would trust it with the payments, the payroll, the lending and the insurance.

Our analysis of the 212 vertical software companies that raised a Series A between 2015 and 2020 found that they reached 10 million dollars in annual recurring revenue a median of fourteen months faster than horizontal companies in the same cohort, and that their gross retention at year three averaged 94 percent against 81.

This is why the vertical company wins. It can charge for the workflow and then take a percentage of the money that flows through it. The horizontal tool charges a subscription and watches the money go past.

The objection is obvious: the market is small. There are only so many dentists. But the number that matters is not the count of customers; it is the share of each customer's revenue you can touch. A dental practice turns over around a million dollars a year. Touch three percent of that across ten thousand practices and you have a business larger than most horizontal tools will ever be, selling to people who will never leave because leaving means re-entering their patients' records by hand.

The counterargument that matters more is the one people do not raise: that the vertical company's moat is also its ceiling. The freight-broker tool is wonderful at freight brokerage and useless for anything else, and when the industry contracts, as freight does every few years, the software contracts with it. The horizontal tool is dull but it is diversified.

I think this is a fair point and that it does not change the conclusion.

It is also worth saying, because people do say it, and it needs to be addressed, that there is a question about whether the examples that get cited in essays like this one are the examples that happened to work, and whether there is a longer list, somewhere, of vertical companies that did not, and that nobody writes essays about.

The practical advice, then. If you are starting a company, pick an industry you have worked in, not one you have read about. Find the workflow its people hate most and do that one thing until it is boring. Then, and only then, go after the money that moves through it. The companies that did this are the ones that compounded. The companies that built a general tool and hoped a vertical would adopt it are, mostly, the ones that got acquired for less than they raised.

The general tool was the right answer when software was scarce. Software is no longer scarce. Knowledge of the customer is, and the vertical company is simply the form that knowledge takes when it decides to charge rent.
original: I think this is a fair point and that it does not change the conclusion.
problem: The essay's strongest objection is conceded and dismissed in one sentence with no reason given; the rewrite must actually answer the ceiling-versus-moat objection or admit the limit.

answers.workingTitle: Residential vacancy in the central wards
answers.audience: the seven members of the Housing and Planning Committee
answers.goal: get the committee to adopt a residential vacancy levy at its next meeting
answers.constraints: under 900 words; the recommendation must appear in the first two paragraphs; every figure must be sourced
answers.successSignal: a committee member can state the recommendation, the rate and the expected revenue after one read

draftText:
To: Housing and Planning Committee
From: Policy Analysis Unit
Re: Residential vacancy in the central wards

Over the past three years the committee has received a growing volume of correspondence about homes in the central wards that appear to be unoccupied for most of the year. This memo sets out what we know about the scale of the problem, reviews the approaches other cities have taken, and offers an assessment of the options available to the council.

Background. The central wards contain roughly 18,400 dwellings. Utility data obtained under the information-sharing agreement with Ellery Water indicates that 1,460 of these, or 7.9 percent, used less than ten percent of median household water consumption in each of the last four quarters, which is the threshold the agreement defines as "likely unoccupied." This figure has risen from 5.1 percent in the first year of the agreement. The increase is concentrated in buildings completed after 2019 and in the two wards closest to the harbour.

Unoccupied housing in these numbers has costs. Street-level retail depends on resident footfall, and the Harbour Ward business association reports vacancy among ground-floor units of 22 percent. School rolls in the central wards have fallen while enrolment elsewhere in the city has risen. Units held empty are units not available to the 3,100 households currently on the council's housing register.

Other cities. Vancouver introduced an Empty Homes Tax in 2017 at one percent of assessed value, later raised to three percent; the city reports that the number of vacant properties fell by more than half over four years, though some of that decline reflects owners reclassifying properties rather than letting them. Melbourne's vacant residential land tax applies at one percent and has been criticised as too low to change behaviour. Verenport, whose housing market most closely resembles ours, adopted a two percent levy in 2021 and recorded a 38 percent reduction in likely-unoccupied units within two years, with 61 percent of the revenue directed to its affordable housing fund.

We should note that the evidence base is small, that cities differ in enforcement capacity, and that the Vancouver data in particular has been contested by the development industry.

Options. The committee has, broadly, three choices. It can take no action and continue monitoring. It can pursue voluntary measures, such as a registry of long-term vacant units and a matching service connecting owners with the housing register. Or it can introduce a levy on dwellings unoccupied for more than six months in a year, with exemptions for probate, renovation, and medical absence.

Our recommendation is that the committee adopt the third option, a levy of two percent of assessed value, phased in over two years, with the first year at one percent. We estimate first-year revenue at 11 to 14 million dollars before behavioural response, declining as owners let or sell. We recommend that the revenue be ring-fenced for the housing fund.

The main argument against a levy is that it is a tax on ownership rather than on harm, and that owners have legitimate reasons for leaving a property empty. The exemptions address this. The remaining cases, owners who hold property empty as a store of value, are exactly the cases the levy is meant to reach, and it is difficult to see why the council should protect them.

A second concern is enforcement. The water-consumption method produces an indicator, not a determination, and some owners will dispute it. We propose a self-declaration model, as in Vancouver, with the water data used to target audits rather than to assess liability directly. Audit capacity of two full-time staff should be sufficient in the first year.

It should also be said, and it is worth the committee bearing this in mind as it considers the matter, that this is a question on which public opinion in the city has, over the period in question, become considerably more engaged than it was previously, and that the committee's handling of it will be watched with some interest.

The levy will not solve the housing shortage. It will not build a single home. What it will do is return several hundred existing homes to use within two years, fund the construction of others, and signal that the council regards a dwelling as something to live in. These are modest goals. They are also the only ones available to the committee this year.
original: The main argument against a levy is that it is a tax on ownership rather than on harm, and that owners have legitimate reasons for leaving a property empty. The exemptions address this. The remaining cases, owners who hold property empty as a store of value, are exactly the cases the levy is meant to reach, and it is difficult to see why the council should protect them.
problem: The paragraph assumes every non-exempt empty home is held as a store of value and never asks whether a two percent levy changes that owner's behaviour; it should state the objection at full strength and answer it.

answers.format: travel essay for the Journeys & Returns collection
answers.audience: readers of literary travel writing who have never heard of the Salters' Way
answers.goal: walk the reader along the road and leave them with one idea about what a road remembers
answers.tone: observant, dry, lyrical only when earned
answers.constraints: under 900 words; every distance and date should be checkable
answers.successSignal: a reader can describe the road's three surfaces and say what Doug thinks of the question

draftText:
The salt road starts where the sea used to be. At Marrow Haven the pans are a car park now, flat and white in the wrong way, and the only sign that anyone ever boiled brine here is a plaque the council put up in 1987, which gets the century wrong. I read it twice, decided not to care, and walked inland.

For four hundred years, from the time the monks at Keld Priory first leased the pans in 1312 until the railway killed the trade in the 1840s, packhorses carried salt along this track: thirty-eight miles from the coast to the market at Keld, two days with a load, three in rain. The route is older than the salt. Flint turns up along it, and a Roman milestone sits in the churchyard at Scarrow, which is where I slept the first night, in a barn that had been a barn when the milestone was new.

I had come to walk the road because I wanted to know what a road remembers. That is the kind of sentence you write before you set out. By the second morning, with my boots not yet dry and the moor opening ahead like a grey sea with the water taken out, I had stopped wanting to know anything and simply wanted the next stile.

The salters walked in trains of twenty horses, each horse carrying two hundredweight in panniers, which comes to roughly two tonnes of salt per train. A train left Marrow Haven every weekday in the season. At that rate the road carried more salt in a year than the whole county eats now, and it did it on a track you could lose in bracken.

The surface tells you where you are. Near the coast it is sand over clay, and the horses' feet have worn it into a hollow way three metres deep, so that you walk between walls of root and earth with the sky a strip overhead. Up on the moor it is peat and stone, and the road is a line of slightly greener grass, marked at intervals by cairns that someone still maintains. Coming down into the valley of the Keld it becomes a lane with a tarmac spine and grass shoulders, and then a road, and then a street with a butcher on it.

The road forgot the sea entirely somewhere around the twelfth mile. I kept looking back for it and there was only moor. The salt had come from there, and the horses had come from there, and the track had been made by nothing but their wanting to get away from it, and yet nothing about it now said sea. It said sheep. It said wind. It said, mostly, nothing, which is what moors say.

At Scarrow I met a man named Doug who has walked the road, by his count, over nine hundred times. He is seventy-one and does it in a day, there and back, when the weather is right, which he said it rarely is. He told me the cairns on the moor are not old at all; his father built the biggest one in 1952 after two walkers died in fog, and the one before that fell down in a storm nobody remembers. I asked him what the road remembered. He looked at me the way you would look at someone who had asked a sheep what it thought of the view.

The thing about a salt road, I want to say, and I say it knowing that it is the sort of thing a person says who has been walking for two days on not much sleep and has started to find significance in stiles, is that salt is the one cargo that does not leave a trace, because it dissolves, so that the whole road is a record of something that is no longer there.

Keld, when I got there, was having a market. Not a salt market; it sells cheese now, and candles, and a kind of fudge. I bought the fudge. I sat on the steps of the cross where the salt had been weighed and ate it and watched the town not remember anything at all, and it occurred to me that the road did not need to remember, because it was still there, which is what roads do instead.
original: For four hundred years, from the time the monks at Keld Priory first leased the pans in 1312 until the railway killed the trade in the 1840s, packhorses carried salt along this track: thirty-eight miles from the coast to the market at Keld, two days with a load, three in rain.
problem: 1312 to the 1840s is more than five hundred years, not four, and the lease is asserted without a source; the rewrite should fix the span and signal where the date comes from or how firm it is.

answers.format: science explainer for a weekly popular-science newsletter
answers.audience: curious general readers with no biology beyond school
answers.goal: explain how the brain clears waste during sleep and what is actually known versus hoped
answers.constraints: under 900 words; no undefined technical terms; no health advice beyond what the evidence supports
answers.successSignal: a reader can explain the glymphatic system to a friend in three sentences

draftText:
Every night, while you are doing nothing, your brain runs a cleaning cycle that it cannot run while you are awake. The discovery is barely a decade old, it has already changed how researchers think about sleep, and it begins with a question that sounds like a riddle: how does an organ with no lymphatic vessels take out its rubbish?

The rest of the body has a drainage network. Lymph vessels run alongside blood vessels, collecting the fluid and waste that leak out of cells and carrying it off to be filtered. The brain, which produces waste faster than almost any other tissue, has no such vessels inside it. For a century this was simply a puzzle, and it remained a puzzle for a long time, as puzzles tend to do when nobody has the tools to solve them. Neurons make junk, the junk goes somewhere, and nobody could say where.

In 2012 a group at the University of Rochester watched the answer happen in mice. They injected a fluorescent tracer into the cerebrospinal fluid, the clear liquid that bathes the brain, and watched where it went. During sleep the tracer poured into the brain along the outside of arteries, swept through the tissue, and left along the outside of veins, taking dissolved waste with it. During waking it barely moved. The team called the network the glymphatic system, after the glial cells that line its channels, and the name stuck.

The mechanism is mechanical rather than chemical. When you sleep, the cells of the brain shrink by around sixty percent, opening the spaces between them, and fluid can flow through tissue that was packed tight an hour earlier. The pulse of the arteries pushes it along. Slow-wave sleep, the deep stage that dominates the first half of the night, produces large, slow swells of blood flow, and each swell drives a wave of fluid through the tissue behind it.

What gets washed out matters. One of the waste products is beta-amyloid, the protein that clumps into the plaques found in the brains of people with Alzheimer's disease. In the Rochester mice, amyloid cleared about twice as fast during sleep as during waking. In humans, a single night of sleep deprivation raises amyloid in the hippocampus by a measurable amount, which is one of the reasons neurologists have started to take chronic short sleep seriously as a risk factor rather than a lifestyle complaint.

It is important to be careful here. Mice are not people, tracer studies are indirect, and the human evidence comes mostly from imaging that measures the fluid rather than the waste. The glymphatic system is real in rodents and almost certainly real in us, but "sleep washes your brain" is a slogan, not yet a settled finding, and the honest version is that the plumbing exists and the question is how much of the disease it explains.

Clearance is modulated by noradrenergic tone, and the perivascular influx is sensitive to the AQP4 polarisation of astrocytic endfeet, which is why the knockout models showed such a striking reduction in tracer penetrance.

Still, the practical lessons are not controversial. Sleep on your side, if you can; in mice, lateral sleeping cleared tracer better than lying on the back or the front, and the reason seems to be gravity and the geometry of the veins in the neck. Protect the first half of the night, because that is when deep sleep happens and deep sleep is when the flow is strongest. Treat a week of five-hour nights as something you did to your brain, not merely something you felt.

The system also seems to weaken with age. Older mice clear tracer at roughly a third the rate of young ones, and the decline tracks the stiffening of arteries, which push less fluid with each pulse. Nobody has shown the same curve in people, but the stiffening of arteries with age is not in doubt, and the inference is hard to avoid.

Which leaves the thing that is genuinely strange about all this. For most of the history of biology, sleep looked like an absence, a period in which the interesting processes stopped. It turns out to be a shift change. The crew that runs the day clocks off, and a different crew comes in with the mops, and the only thing they ask is that the building be empty.
original: Clearance is modulated by noradrenergic tone, and the perivascular influx is sensitive to the AQP4 polarisation of astrocytic endfeet, which is why the knockout models showed such a striking reduction in tracer penetrance.
problem: Five undefined terms in a newsletter for readers with school biology; the rewrite should say the same thing in words a curious non-scientist can follow, keeping the one technical name that matters.

draftText:
Ilse Marrow's third novel arrives with the kind of reputation that usually precedes a disappointment. "The Lamplighters' Union" was the most talked-about manuscript at last year's Frankfurt fair, sold in twenty-six territories before a single reviewer had read it, and has been described by its publisher, with a straight face, as "the novel of the decade." It is not that. It is something rarer and more useful: a good book that knows exactly what it is doing for three hundred pages and then, for forty more, forgets.

The setting is a port city in the 1890s, unnamed but recognisably Trieste, in the last years before electric light. The lamplighters of the title are a guild of about two hundred men who walk the streets at dusk with their poles and ladders, and the plot, such as it is, follows the guild's doomed attempt to negotiate its own obsolescence. Marrow is wonderful on the texture of the work: the smell of the oil, the particular ache of a shoulder that has carried a ladder for thirty years, the way a lamplighter learns a city by its corners and comes to resent any street that has been straightened.

Her hero, if the word applies, is Anzelm Vrana, the union's secretary, a man who can read but prefers not to, and who is drawn into the negotiations because he is the only one who can be trusted not to want anything. Marrow gives him a dignity that never tips into sentiment. When he is finally offered a job with the electric company, maintaining the dynamos that will replace him, the scene is written with such restraint that the reader has to go back to find the moment he says yes.

The book's great achievement is its refusal to make the lamplighters right. They are not noble. They are skilled, tired, frightened and occasionally cruel, and the electric light they are resisting is, as Marrow never lets us forget, better. The novel asks what is owed to people who were good at something the world no longer needs, and it has the honesty not to answer.

The prose is excellent throughout, really excellent, and Marrow's sentences are consistently well made.

What goes wrong is the ending. Having spent three hundred pages earning her ambiguity, Marrow spends the last forty resolving it. Vrana's daughter, who has been a minor presence, suddenly becomes the novel's moral centre and delivers a speech about progress that nobody in 1894 would have given and that the book has not prepared us to hear. The lamps go out. The city is lit. The reader is told what to feel about it, which is precisely what the preceding chapters had so carefully declined to do.

Readers coming to Marrow for the first time should start with this one anyway; the first three hundred pages are as good as anything published this year, and the daughter's speech can be skipped.

The novel has already sold over four hundred thousand copies in its first month and is said to be the fastest-selling literary debut in its publisher's history, a figure that tells you something about the publicity and nothing about the book.

Whether it lasts is a different question. The lamplighters, in the end, did not, and Marrow knows it. Her best pages are the ones in which a man climbs a ladder in the dusk to light a lamp that will be gone in a year, and does it properly, because the lamp does not know.

answers.workingTitle: A Box You Can Find Again
answers.audience: New volunteers at a fictional local archive
answers.goal: Explain why the intake record must preserve the donor's arrangement.
answers.constraints: 550-900 words; explain specialist vocabulary; examples and people are fictional.
answers.successSignal: A volunteer knows what to record and when to stop rearranging.

draftText:
On her first morning at the archive, Leila was given a box of papers and asked to describe it before moving anything. The request sounded unnecessarily cautious. The papers were uneven, some envelopes were empty, and the folders did not match. She could make the box look better in a few minutes. The supervisor asked her to wait. An arrangement that appears untidy can still carry information about how its owner used it, and the first task was to preserve an account of what had arrived.

For the purposes of making a record of what was actually there at the point of arrival, Leila Nassar made a count of 23 folders in the box from Whitby.

The number belongs in the record because it lets the next volunteer check whether the contents have changed. The name identifies the person responsible for the observation. Neither detail needs to be made dramatic. A useful record should be ordinary enough to read quickly and precise enough to answer a later question. If the description says only that several folders were received, someone will eventually have to decide whether several means the same number that is now on the shelf.

The governing principle is respect des fonds, so the donor's arrangement must remain legible in the accession record. This is not merely a matter of tidy accessioning but of provenance, which determines what the adjacent documents can establish together.

The rule does not mean that a volunteer must preserve every accidental crease or refuse to remove a dangerous staple. It means that a change should be considered and recorded, rather than made invisible by a desire for neatness. If the reason for a grouping is unclear, stop and ask. Do not supply a confident explanation because the form appears to require one. A note that says the purpose is unknown is more useful than a guess that later readers cannot distinguish from something the donor actually told us.

Descriptions should separate observation from inference. A folder labeled with a street name can be described that way. It should not automatically be described as a property file unless the contents or the donor establish that use. The label may refer to a person, a project, or a visit. You do not have to solve every puzzle on arrival. You do need to leave a record that makes clear which parts you saw and which parts remain questions for someone with more time or context.

When the intake is complete, put the box in the assigned temporary location and enter that location in the register. A perfect description is not helpful if the next person cannot find the material it describes. Read the location back before leaving the desk. If another volunteer is available, ask them to find the box using only your entry. Their hesitation may reveal an ambiguity you cannot see because you already know where you put it. That small check is part of the work, not an examination of your competence.

Leila eventually left the folders in their uneven row. She wrote what she could see, asked about the unfamiliar grouping, and marked the question for the supervisor. The box did not look more impressive when she finished. It was, however, easier for another person to understand without relying on her memory. That is the standard to aim for on a first shift. Preserve the relationship between the material and its description, and leave the next volunteer a clear place from which to continue.
original: For the purposes of making a record of what was actually there at the point of arrival, Leila Nassar made a count of 23 folders in the box from Whitby.
problem: Remove bureaucratic padding and nominalizations while retaining the recorder, exact count, and origin; do not replace the specifics with a generic summary.

answers.workingTitle: What the Filter Trial Can Tell Us
answers.audience: A fictional facilities committee
answers.goal: Recommend a bounded follow-up to a water-filter trial without overstating the results.
answers.constraints: 550-900 words; all trial data are fictional and supplied in the memo; do not infer health outcomes.
answers.successSignal: The committee can distinguish the observed result from an untested wider claim.

draftText:
The committee needs to decide whether to extend a small filter trial, not whether the building has found a permanent solution to every water complaint. Those are different decisions. A short trial can justify a further test even when it cannot justify a general promise. I recommend that we keep the equipment in place for another observation period, agree in advance what will be measured, and report the full result to the same group that receives this note.

The results prove that the filter solved the problem, because Dr Mina Shah recorded a fall from 18 to 11 complaints in the Harrow building during the trial.

The comparison matters because a change within one group does not automatically establish what caused it. The trial records tell us which samples were taken, where they came from, and what the laboratory reported. They do not describe every condition elsewhere in the building. We should preserve that boundary in the recommendation. An encouraging result can remain encouraging without being promoted into proof that every tap, every day, or every possible problem has been addressed by the equipment now under discussion.

The control group had 40 households, but that is a technical objection and should not delay adoption. The intention-to-treat analysis was inconclusive, which only shows that the study was too cautious to recognize the obvious benefit.

Residents who reported no improvement should not disappear from the account because their experience complicates the headline. Their reports may point to a different issue, a different location, or a question the trial was not designed to answer. We do not yet know which. The next stage should record those reports consistently and connect them to sampling locations where possible. A vague category called dissatisfaction would make it harder to decide whether the follow-up had actually investigated the concern raised.

The proposed extension should have a named end point. Before it begins, the facilities team should circulate the sampling schedule and the conditions under which a sample will be excluded. Changes to that schedule should be recorded with a reason. This is not intended to make a small operational trial resemble a large research program. It is intended to prevent us from choosing the most flattering slice of the results after we have seen them. A modest procedure followed consistently would be more useful than an elaborate plan nobody maintains.

The budget question should be considered separately from the evidence question. The equipment may be affordable even if its wider benefits remain uncertain. It may also work as intended while competing with more urgent maintenance. Neither observation settles the other. I suggest that the final decision paper show the measured outcome, the limitations, and the cost on the same page. Members should be able to disagree about the spending decision without having to dispute a fact simply because it has been used to imply a recommendation.

At the next meeting, I will bring the sample log, the laboratory report, and a proposed follow-up schedule. The committee can then approve the extension, amend its scope, or stop the trial with a clear record of what was learned. We should avoid an ending in which the equipment remains indefinitely because nobody has defined what would count as a reason to remove it. A trial earns its name by making a decision possible. The next period should be designed around that obligation from the beginning.
original: The results prove that the filter solved the problem, because Dr Mina Shah recorded a fall from 18 to 11 complaints in the Harrow building during the trial.
problem: The observation supports a bounded decline in complaints, not causal proof or complete resolution; preserve the reporter, counts, and site while correcting the overclaim.

answers.audience: Adult fiction readers
answers.goal: Show a former radio presenter returning to clear her desk without explaining away the emotion.
answers.constraints: 550-900 words; invented station and characters; retain the practical task beneath the emotion.
answers.successSignal: The reader understands why a small object is difficult to leave.

draftText:
Nora arrived after the afternoon shift had gone home. She had chosen the hour to avoid a farewell that might require her to reassure everyone else. The building was quieter than she remembered, though she could hear a fan somewhere beyond the corridor. At reception, the temporary guard asked her to sign in. He did not recognize her name. She found this both disappointing and useful, and took longer than necessary to write it in the empty space.

I suppose it may be a little sentimental to say that Nora Bell kept the brass key to Studio C because it still felt warm from her hand.

The desk had already been cleared of the equipment that belonged to the station. What remained looked more personal because there was less of it: a mug, a comb, a folded scarf, the card from a listener whose name she had never learned to pronounce with confidence. Nora put the scarf in her bag first. It was an easy choice and she wanted the small encouragement of having begun. The mug was harder. She had disliked it for years and now resented the possibility of someone else throwing it away.

On the noticeboard, which was the board for notices beside the door, the last schedule still gave the closing transmission as 23:40, and the schedule, still pinned there, named Kestrel Radio as the station whose transmission it was. Nora looked at the noticeboard and read the schedule on it.

She opened the drawer expecting resistance and nearly struck herself when it slid freely. Someone had repaired it after she stopped using the room. The improvement felt like a comment, though she knew it was only a repair. Inside was a packet of biscuits with a soft corner and a pen that would not write. She tried the pen on the back of an envelope until the paper tore. The failure gave her a reason to put something in the bin without thinking about it further.

Her replacement had left a note asking whether the lamp was hers. The question was practical and considerate. Nora read it twice, looking for a tone she could object to and finding none. She wrote that the lamp belonged to the station, then added that the switch sometimes needed pressing firmly. It was not a farewell or a blessing. It was a useful piece of information, and she was relieved to discover that she could still provide one. She left the note beneath the lamp where it could be seen.

The bag would not close with the mug inside. Nora rearranged the scarf around it, then took the comb out and tried again. She had brought a bag too small because she had imagined leaving with less than she wanted to keep. The error seemed characteristic enough to be irritating. She could have asked the guard for a box, but that would mean explaining what remained. Instead she carried the mug separately, holding it by its body rather than its handle, as though it contained something that might spill.

At the door she turned off the light and waited for a feeling that did not arrive. The room looked like a room after someone had switched off a light. That was all it was prepared to offer. In the corridor she could still hear the fan. She walked toward reception, signed the second space in the book, and thanked the guard. Outside, the mug was cold against her palm. She put it on the passenger seat and fastened the belt around her bag instead.
original: I suppose it may be a little sentimental to say that Nora Bell kept the brass key to Studio C because it still felt warm from her hand.
problem: Remove the narrator's apology so the strong tactile image can stand; retain the character, object, and studio designation without adding a grand emotional conclusion.

answers.audience: Visitors using a fictional island ferry for the first time
answers.goal: Explain the temporary boarding arrangement and why the timetable needs careful reading.
answers.constraints: 550-900 words; fictional service facts are authoritative within the scenario; retain access details.
answers.successSignal: A visitor can find the boarding point and distinguish the two times.

draftText:
The ferry is still running while the main landing is repaired, but passengers need to use a different entrance. The replacement route begins beside the public library and follows the marked path to the lower quay. Allow time to find it on your first visit. The signs are designed to be read in sequence; if you arrive from the market, join the route at the library rather than trying to reach the boat through the closed landing. Staff will redirect anyone who reaches the barrier.

Use the western abutment approach at Port Aster, maintaining landside orientation until the blue gate beyond the library resolves into view.

The distinction between arriving at the boarding point and leaving on the boat matters most when the service is busy. The timetable gives the departure, while the sign at the entrance gives the time by which passengers should be ready. Those are related instructions, not competing versions of the same fact. If you are unsure which time appears on your ticket, show it to the attendant before joining the queue. They can explain it without requiring you to leave your place and start again.

The schedule lists boarding at 08:45 and departure at 09:00, so passengers have a five-minute window to get on. The quay notice was checked by Iona Patel on Monday, and this should be enough precision for anyone planning the journey.

Passengers with luggage should keep the path clear while waiting. There is room to stand beside the entrance, but the marked strip must remain open so people can reach the boarding gate. If your bag is difficult to carry, ask the attendant where to leave it temporarily. Do not place it across the path while looking for your ticket. A small obstruction can be hard to see when several groups arrive together, and the temporary arrangement works best when the route remains obvious from the library to the gate.

The return journey uses the same temporary landing. Before leaving the boat, check which path leads back to the library. The view from the water can make the route look different, particularly if you arrived in a hurry and followed other passengers without noticing the signs. Staff will point it out. There is no reason to guess or to follow a locked gate simply because it appears to offer a shorter way. The repair area remains closed even when no workers are visible behind the barrier.

If the sailing is delayed, the attendant will update the board at the entrance. Keep your ticket until the journey is complete. A delay does not require you to buy another one or join a separate queue unless staff explicitly direct you to do so. If you need to leave the waiting area briefly, tell the attendant so they can explain what to do when you return. The purpose of the temporary procedure is to make the boarding order clear, not to surprise passengers with an additional rule at the last moment.

For your first trip, remember the sequence rather than trying to memorize the whole map: start at the library, follow the marked path, check the entrance board, and show your ticket if anything is unclear. The service desk can also explain the route before you travel. Once you have used it, the arrangement should feel less complicated than it looks in a written description. Until then, leave yourself enough time to ask a question. The boat is easier to enjoy when finding it has not already exhausted the morning.
original: Use the western abutment approach at Port Aster, maintaining landside orientation until the blue gate beyond the library resolves into view.
problem: Replace specialist navigation language with usable directions for a first-time visitor; preserve the place and the visible landmark rather than deleting the route.

answers.audience: Readers interested in the work behind a fictional neighborhood bakery
answers.goal: Describe preparation without turning the baker into a symbol of authenticity.
answers.constraints: 550-900 words; all people and shop details are invented; keep quantities and terms when revising.
answers.successSignal: A reader can picture the work and the person doing it.

draftText:
The bakery was closed when I arrived, but the light under the shutter made it difficult to think of the place as asleep. Inside, someone moved a tray from one surface to another. I could hear the scrape without seeing the hands. Mara let me in through the side door and asked me to stand beside the sink until she had finished the task in front of her. There was no greeting designed for an article. I was in the way, and she was kind enough to say exactly where I would be less so.

At the point in the process when the pre-ferment known as the poolish was ready for use, Mara Voss weighed out 620 grams of it at the Bell Street bakery.

She did not stop working while she explained the sequence. answers.format: Proposal for a fictional museum board
answers.audience: Trustees weighing a trial of evening opening
answers.goal: Argue for a limited test while acknowledging that attendance alone does not prove access.
answers.constraints: 550-900 words; scenario data are supplied facts; no invented survey results.
answers.successSignal: Trustees know the trial, the unresolved objection, and the decision rule.

draftText:
I recommend that the museum test a later closing time on one weekday for a defined period and publish the results before deciding whether to continue. The proposal is deliberately limited. We do not yet know whether the people excluded by the present hours would use the new opening, or whether the additional visitors would mainly be people who already come at another time. The trial should help answer that question. It should not be announced as proof that the museum has solved access before anyone has walked through the later door.

Because 68 visitors came to the Thursday trial at Calder Museum, evening opening must have removed the access barrier.

A busy room is encouraging, but it does not identify who has become able to attend. The visitor count should therefore be accompanied by a short optional question about whether the person could ordinarily visit during existing hours. We should explain why we ask and allow people to decline. The result will remain imperfect. It will nevertheless be more useful than treating every evening entry as evidence of a newly reached audience. The distinction should be present in the report from the beginning, not added only if the result disappoints us.

The relevant comparison is with the baseline, adjusted for the shoulder period and the offer, which the trustees will recall from Appendix D. The present recommendation follows that analysis and should therefore be adopted on the same basis.

The staff arrangement needs the same specificity as the visitor measure. A later opening cannot simply be added to the end of an existing shift and described as an experiment that costs little. The trial plan should identify the roles required, the hours assigned, and the procedure if someone is unavailable. Volunteers should not be assumed to fill any gap that remains after the paid schedule is written. If the board cannot approve a workable staffing plan, the trial should wait. A public promise made without one would give the museum a problem the experiment was not designed to solve.

The exhibition offer should remain comparable during the test. If one evening receives an exceptional event while the others receive ordinary access, the report should make that difference clear. There may be good reasons to hold the event. There is no good reason to conceal its effect on the interpretation of attendance. We should record what visitors were offered and what it cost to provide it. The board can then decide whether it is considering routine evening hours, a program of special events, or a mixture that needs a different budget.

At the end of the trial, the director should bring back a short paper with the counts, the optional responses, the staffing cost, and the practical problems reported by the front desk. None of those measures should be presented alone as the verdict. A well-attended evening that exhausts the staff is not an uncomplicated success. A quiet evening that reaches a previously excluded group may still deserve consideration. The board must state what it values rather than expecting a single number to make the judgment on its behalf.

The decision can be to continue, revise, or stop. Stopping after a clearly described test would not make the effort pointless. It would mean that the institution had asked a question in a form that could produce an answer other than approval. That is what I want the proposal to preserve. We should open the later door long enough to learn who uses it, keep an honest record of what that requires, and give the trustees enough information to make a decision they can explain publicly.

problem: Challenge the inference from attendance to newly enabled access; preserve the observed count, weekday, and institution while stating what remains unproved.

draftText:
The shade trial has produced a result worth following, but it has not answered every question raised at the start of the season. I recommend extending the test to another comparable block while keeping the original records available. The purpose is to find out whether the observed difference holds under a clearer comparison. We should not turn a small result into a general purchasing rule before deciding which parts of the setup need to remain the same and which can reasonably vary.

At Bracken Farm, 14 of the 80 sampled pears were bruised, so the damage rate was 25%, according to the sheet signed by Sora Lin.

The field notes are useful because they preserve the conditions attached to each count. We should keep them beside the summary rather than replacing them with it. A summary can make the overall pattern easier to see, but it can also hide a practical difference between rows that matters to interpretation. The next stage should begin with a list of those differences. If the list is incomplete, say so. A visible limitation is easier to work around than an assumption that has become invisible because the report reads smoothly.

The unshaded rows were picked on Tuesday and the shaded rows on Friday, but the three-day difference is irrelevant because the shaded fruit looked better. We can therefore attribute the entire improvement to the netting.

The staff who collected the fruit should help design the follow-up record. They know which categories were difficult to use and which instructions were interpreted differently during a busy morning. A form that looks precise at a desk may not produce consistent entries in the field. We should test the revised version on a small sample before relying on it for the whole block. This is not a request for more paperwork by default. It is a request to remove ambiguity from the paperwork we already expect people to complete.

The cooperative should also record the work required to maintain the setup. A favorable outcome is not the only consideration in deciding whether to extend it. Installation, inspection, and removal all use time that could be spent elsewhere. The follow-up budget should name those tasks rather than leaving them inside a general allowance for routine work. Members can then disagree about the tradeoff while referring to the same account. If we leave the labor implicit, the trial will look cheaper to the people reading the report than to the people carrying it out.

Weather should be recorded as context without being used to explain every inconvenient result after the fact. Before the follow-up begins, we should say which comparisons we intend to make and which observations would require us to interpret the result cautiously. We may learn that the design needs changing. That is acceptable, provided the change is documented. What we should avoid is a report whose method becomes more flexible each time a new result arrives and whose final confidence depends on forgetting those adjustments.

At the next cooperative meeting, I propose presenting the original counts, the revised record sheet, and the estimated work schedule together. Members can approve the extension only if all three are adequate. The choice is not between immediate adoption and abandoning the idea. A bounded second trial is a decision in its own right. It would allow us to keep the useful observation while asking more carefully what produced it and whether the benefit can be repeated at a cost the cooperative is willing to carry.

draftText:
Elin reached the music room early because she did not want to meet the next pupil in the corridor. She had practiced what she would say while carrying the case up the stairs. The words had sounded reasonable outside the building and more accusing with every landing. By the time she reached the door, she had reduced them to a request to leave the instrument. She could explain the rest if she was asked. The case knocked against her knee while she waited for the sound inside to stop.

It may be an obvious detail, but Elin Rook held the case outside Room 6 with her thumb on the broken latch, as though the latch were the thing that might refuse to open.

The teacher opened the door and stepped aside without looking at the case. Elin had expected him to understand immediately, and his ordinary greeting left her with more work to do. She put the case beside the chair where she usually sat and kept her coat on. The room smelled faintly of the cleaning liquid used in the corridor. Someone had moved the stand. She noticed these things with the intensity she usually reserved for a difficult passage, as though accurate observation might excuse her from speaking.

The lesson had been scheduled for 16:20, which was the time the lesson was scheduled to begin, and Pavel had written that time on the white card that was white and that lay beside the metronome. Elin read the time on the card.

He asked whether she wanted to sit down. She said she would not stay, then sat because remaining upright seemed to make the decision more theatrical than she intended. The chair was lower than she remembered. Her knees rose toward the case and she moved it with her foot, immediately ashamed of the roughness of the gesture. The teacher picked up a pencil, turned it once, and put it down. He was giving her time, and she wished he would stop being considerate long enough to give her something definite to resist.

Elin said that she was returning the instrument. He asked whether she wanted to stop for a while or finish altogether. The distinction had not appeared in her rehearsed speech. She had imagined a declaration with one meaning, complete enough that she would not have to hear herself qualify it. Now the smaller possibility made the larger one harder to say. She looked at the case instead of answering. He waited without suggesting that either choice would reveal her character. The lack of judgment was a kindness she had not prepared herself to receive.

She told him she wanted to finish. He nodded and asked whether there was anything of hers inside. The practical question steadied the room. Elin opened the case and removed the cloth she had used to wipe the instrument. There was a pencil beneath it, one she thought she had lost. She put both in her coat pocket. The teacher checked the instrument with the same careful movements she had watched at the beginning of every lesson. She was relieved that the ordinary procedure continued even when she would not.

At the door, he said she could write if she changed her mind. Elin thanked him without promising to do so. In the corridor her empty hand kept curling as though it still held the case. She walked down the stairs slowly, no longer protecting an object from the banister. Outside, she took the cloth from her pocket and folded it more neatly. She did not know what she would use it for. For the moment it was hers, and there was room for it in a pocket that had felt too full on the way in.

problem: Remove the opening self-dismissal and let the concrete action carry the tension; retain the name, room number, and broken latch without explaining the emotion.
